newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire governor says no refugee airlift until May 5.
newsitem.headline: Zaire governor says no refugee airlift until May 5.

text.p: A United Nations plan to repatriate Rwandan Hutu refugees, already delayed by logistical problems, disease and opposition from local residents, was further postponed on Sunday until at least May.
The governor of Eastern Province (formerly Upper Zaire), Yagi Sitolo, said the operation should not start until May 5 because of a cholera epidemic.
The governor intervened last week to delay a plan to start an airlift this weekend of up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from two jungle camps south of Kisangani.
His reason then was that a cholera outbreak among the refugees threatened local Zaireans.
"If the epidemic is well controlled, it should die down by May 5 and we could start repatriation," Sitolo told Reuters in Kisangani on Sunday.
"But for medical reasons it shouldn't start before then," said Sitolo, a medical doctor elected with the blessing of rebels last month.

About 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have been living in horrific conditions at Biaro and Kasese camps since rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/ Zaire (AFDL) captured Kisangani on March 15.
The death toll from cholera, malaria and malnutrition stands at around 40 a day, with bodies lined up under blankets along a mud road leading through the camps.
Aid workers on Sunday accused Zairean rebels of playing games with the lives of Rwandan refugees and said many faced death because of delays in their repatriation.

"The situation at the moment is completely unacceptable," one aid worker told Reuters. "We need to put pressure on the Alliance (rebels), on governments, on whoever it takes to get those people out of there."
Sitolo said residents were already at risk from the cholera outbreak at Kasese camp and would be in even greater danger if refugees were driven by truck to Kisangani airport for repatriation.
The water supply to surrounding villages was polluted by the burial of cholera-infected bodies, he said, and he challenged aid workers to drink the water used by villagers.
"I want the refugees to go home. But I must also look after the local population who are very fragile," Sitolo said.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR has dismissed such fears as groundless, and an official from the U.S.-based Centers for Disease Control flew to Kisangani on Saturday to add weight to the argument.
"At the moment they (the authorities) are just playing games with people's lives," one aid worker said.
Twenty-three new cholera cases were reported on Friday, bringing the total to 408 since mid-March. Some 42 people have died from the disease, according to UNHCR figures.
Angry local people broke the windscreen of a U.N. vehicle returning from the camps on Saturday on the second day of protests against the refugees and the presence of aid workers.
Privately, aid officials say they fear the protests may be orchestrated by the Alliance to cover up a shift in policy over the planned repatriation. Sitolo denied this.
Aid officials speculated that Rwanda could be becoming overwhelmed by the continuing flood of returning refugees, and so was putting pressure on the Alliance to halt the repatriation.
Alternatively, they say, the prevarication could indicate a split between rebel leaders and local Zairean leaders.

More than a million Hutu refugees fled East Zaire camps last October and November, at the start of the advance by rebels who control more than half of the vast country and are threatening the capital Kinshasa.

Most refugees returned home from Zaire in November but hundreds of thousands fled west -- including members of the former Rwandan army and the militia held responsible for massacres during the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
